package_info.package_versions: 2023 version 18.3 and earlier; 2022 version 17.4.1 and earlier
package_info.why_malicious: Multiple vulnerabilities in the InDesign plugin allow attackers to exploit malformed QuarkXPress Drawing (QXD) files, leading to memory leaks or arbitrary code execution. These vulnerabilities enable attackers to execute code or leak sensitive information by simply opening a crafted file, which is a critical security risk.

execution_context.file_location: InDesign plugin responsible for decoding QuarkXPress Drawing (QXD) files

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: if (qxd_file.length > MAX_SIZE) { ... } // improper bounds check leading to out-of-bounds write
malicious_snippets.code_language: C++ (likely, as per Adobe plugin development)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When a QXD file is opened, the code fails to properly check the bounds of the file data, allowing a crafted file to cause an out-of-bounds memory write, resulting in arbitrary code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Out-of-bounds writes are a classic vector for arbitrary code execution, especially when triggered by untrusted file input.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal file parsing should strictly validate all input sizes and boundaries; here, the code allows unchecked writes based on attacker-controlled data.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate plugins may parse complex file formats, but must always enforce strict bounds checking.
key_indicators: Improper bounds check on file input
Triggered by opening a crafted file

execution_context.file_location: InDesign plugin responsible for decoding QuarkXPress Drawing (QXD) files

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: data = qxd_file[offset]; // improper bounds check leading to out-of-bounds read
malicious_snippets.code_language: C++ (likely, as per Adobe plugin development)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When a QXD file is opened, the code fails to properly check the bounds of the file data, allowing a crafted file to cause an out-of-bounds memory read, resulting in leakage of sensitive information from process memory.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Out-of-bounds reads can leak sensitive data, such as memory contents, which may include credentials or other secrets.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal file parsing should never allow reading outside the allocated buffer; this behavior exposes internal memory to attackers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate plugins may read file data, but must always enforce strict bounds checking.
key_indicators: Improper bounds check on file input
Triggered by opening a crafted file

attack_chain.action: Attacker crafts a malicious QXD file with malformed data to exploit improper bounds checks.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious file is delivered to the victim (e.g., via email, download, or shared drive).

attack_chain.action: Victim opens the malicious QXD file in Adobe InDesign.
attack_chain.leads_to: InDesign plugin processes the file, triggering the vulnerabilities.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code executes: either arbitrary code execution (snippet_1) or sensitive memory leakage (snippet_2).
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains code execution or access to leaked information.

behavioral_signatures: Opening QXD files triggers unexpected memory access violations
InDesign process attempts to execute code from memory regions associated with file input
Unusual memory reads or writes during QXD file parsing
file_indicators: QXD files with malformed or oversized data sections
QXD files that cause crashes or exceptions in InDesign
network_indicators: Not directly applicable unless attacker payload includes network exfiltration; monitor for suspicious outbound connections from InDesign process after opening QXD files
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for InDesign process crashes or exceptions when opening QXD files, especially those involving access violations. Use endpoint protection to detect exploitation attempts (e.g., memory corruption, code execution). Scan QXD files for malformed structures or oversized fields. Employ IPS/EDR signatures for known exploit patterns targeting these vulnerabilities.
